content: The findings from the declarations of interest (DOI) submitted by participating experts were handled in strict accordance with WHO procedures. This ensured that the work of WHO and the contributions of its experts were both genuinely and transparently objective and independent. The names and biographies of the experts were made publicly available online two weeks before the meeting. In cases where a conflict of interest was deemed insignificant and unlikely to compromise the guideline development process or its credibility, the experts were only required to disclose such conflicts openly at the beginning of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting or prior to their participation as external reviewers. No further actions were taken in these cases. During the GDG meeting, the group reviewed and discussed the evidence summaries and sought clarifications where necessary. In addition to assessing the balance between the desirable and undesirable effects of the intervention and the overall certainty of the evidence, the GDG applied additional criteria from the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework. These criteria included stakeholder values, resource implications, acceptability, feasibility, and equity. The group’s considerations were informed by the expertise and opinions of its members and supported by evidence from literature searches where available. EtD tables were used to organize and synthesize these considerations. Decisions were made by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of the participants. None of the GDG members opposed the recommendations. Before the online meeting, the WHO Steering Group prepared draft versions of the GRADE evidence profiles, evidence summaries, and other relevant documents for the GDG’s deliberations. These drafts were shared with participants two weeks before the meeting for their comments. During the meeting, the documents were revised based on the participants’ discussions and feedback. After the meeting, the WHO Steering Group drafted the final recommendation document to accurately reflect the deliberations and decisions of the participants. This draft was then sent electronically to GDG members and the External Review Group for final review and approval. Following the GDG’s review and approval, the final document was sent to eight external independent experts (the External Review Group) for peer review. The WHO Steering Group evaluated the feedback from these reviewers for inclusion in the document. Any modifications made after the meeting and external peer review were limited to correcting factual errors and improving language clarity. The GDG recommended that women with non-severe hypertension during pregnancy should be offered antihypertensive drug treatment as part of high-quality antenatal care. Oral alpha-agonists (e.g., methyldopa) and beta-blockers were identified as effective treatment options for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy. The use of antihypertensive drugs in this context likely reduces the risk of developing severe hypertension, although it may have little or no effect on the risk of proteinuria or pre-eclampsia. There may be a slight increase in side effects associated with antihypertensive drug use. While several antihypertensive drugs have been evaluated, there is insufficient evidence to determine which drug is superior. Methyldopa likely reduces severe hypertension compared to placebo or no treatment. Beta-blockers likely reduce the onset of severe hypertension and pre-eclampsia but may increase side effects. Calcium channel blockers likely increase the risk of proteinuria or pre-eclampsia. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and sodium nitroprusside should be avoided due to safety concerns. The GDG emphasized that pregnant women prescribed antihypertensive drugs require regular outpatient monitoring and review by antenatal care providers. Access to antenatal care services for monitoring blood pressure, complications (e.g., proteinuria), and treatment side effects is essential when initiating antihypertensive treatment. Methyldopa was highlighted as having the fewest safety concerns, being listed in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, and being widely available in many countries. Available evidence suggests that calcium channel blockers should be avoided. The choice of antihypertensive drug should be tailored to the woman’s clinical situation, considering pre-existing treatment, side effect profiles, risks (including potential fetal effects), cost, local availability, and the woman’s preferences. The recommendations will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, WHO collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. They will also be available on the WHO website and in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. Updated recommendations will be shared during meetings and scientific conferences attended by relevant WHO staff. The document will be translated into the six UN languages and disseminated through WHO regional offices. Technical assistance will be provided to regional offices willing to translate the full recommendations into these languages. Successful implementation of these recommendations into national programs and healthcare services depends on well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes of adaptation and implementation. This may involve developing or revising existing national guidelines or protocols. The recommendations should be adapted into locally appropriate documents to meet the specific needs of each country and healthcare service. Changes should be made transparently and explicitly. Interventions should ensure an enabling environment for the use of these recommendations, including the availability of antihypertensive drugs and access to antenatal care. Healthcare providers working in antenatal care settings require training and supportive supervision on prescribing antihypertensive drugs appropriately and safely, as well as on informing and counseling women about the risks and benefits of available options. Implementation should be monitored at the health-service level as part of broader efforts to improve the quality of maternal and newborn care. This can involve clinical audits or criterion-based clinical reviews to monitor indicators such as the proportion of women with non-severe hypertension who received antihypertensive drug therapy and the proportion of pregnant women with non-severe hypertension who progressed to more severe disease or experienced adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes. Monitoring should align with the standards and indicators described in the WHO document Standards for improving quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities. The recommendations will be reviewed annually by the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) to assess WHO’s portfolio of maternal and perinatal health recommendations and advise on prioritization for new and existing questions. If new evidence emerges that could impact the current evidence base, the recommendations may be updated. If no new evidence is identified, the recommendations may be revalidated. Following publication and dissemination, any concerns about the validity of the recommendations will be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, and plans will be made to update the recommendations if necessary. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in future updates.
